The View from SomewherePart IV · Inference at the edge

Chapter 15

A statistic with a kink

Web edition. Figure 15.2 is live: you can resize the survey, move the corner and draw again.

In cycle 15 we had a test that looked like the useful result of Part III. It was built on the estimated shortfall C^ of Chapters 13 and 14, and in the four cells of our design where the null is true it declared incoherence in at most 4.5 percent of 200 samples. At the largest drift it caught 97 percent of incoherent systems at n=1000, against 61 percent for the rule it replaced. Then we looked at the critical values. The 95th percentile of the null distribution was zero in every sample we inspected, so the calibrated test was the rule declare incoherence when C^>0. That seemed a strange thing to be right.

It was not right. Cycle 16 put the rule where it should be hardest to pass, with the truth exactly on the edge of the null, and where a drift had used up the slack in the margins it raised false alarms in 7.5 to 24.3 percent of samples across four drifts and three sample sizes. Cycle 17 then explained why, and the explanation fits in a picture: the statistic has a corner, the corner sits exactly where the truth is, and no amount of data rounds it off. By the end of the chapter you will have seen the corner, sampled around it, watched the standard bootstrap fail to see it, and read what Fang and Santos proved about that. You will also have the record of what we got wrong on the way, because three of the corrections in this chapter came from an independent review of our own claims.

Here is all that Chapters 13 and 14 contribute. A system of three tables on ordered answers has a cut shortfall C≥0, which is zero exactly when the tables could come from one population in which every shared variable is allowed to drift across each cut in only one direction. The null of the whole program is C=0. Write D for the least total expected distance between copies of the shared variables over all populations that reproduce the tables, and W for the transport distance between the shared margins, which can be read off the tables. Chapter 14 proves the identity D=W+2C,soC=12(D−W).D=W+2C,soC=12(D−W). The estimate C^ is the same expression computed from sample tables. Everything below uses only two things about it: C is never negative, and it is built from a linear program and some absolute values.

15.1A function with a corner

Take a function ϕ of the tables p, and a point p0 with ϕ(p0)=0. The delta method needs a derivative. When there is none, there is often a directional derivative, ϕp0′(h)=limt↓0ϕ(p0+th)−ϕ(p0)t, and for a Lipschitz ϕ, as every function in this chapter is, ϕ is fully differentiable at p0 exactly when this map of h is linear.

The shortfall C has directional derivatives, and the reason is elementary. D is the optimal value of a linear program in which the tables enter as the right-hand side, so it is a convex and piecewise linear function of them; W is a sum of absolute values of linear functions, so it is piecewise linear too; hence so is C=(D−W)/2. (In the first write-up we marked directional differentiability as unchecked. The notebook later corrects that: it is the standard fact about linear program values, and every valid set of tables lies in the domain where it holds. What we have not checked is a different matter, taken up in the section on the papers.)

Now use the one fact that makes this useful. C≥0 everywhere, and C(p0)=0. Then C(p0+th)≥0 for every direction h and every small t, so Cp0′(h) ≥ 0for every h.Cp0′(h) ≥ 0for every h. A map that is linear and non-negative in every direction is zero: put h and −h in and the two values must add to zero, so both are zero. So if there is any direction in which C leaves zero at first order, Cp0′ is not linear, and C is not differentiable at p0. A point on the boundary of the null is by definition such a point. Because C is piecewise linear, C(p0+th)=tCp0′(h) for small t, so these are the directions in which a small step makes C positive, and the corner is made of the places where Cp0′ switches between being zero and being positive.

Real tables are high-dimensional, so here is a small invented function with the same structure; nothing in it comes from the research. Three categories have probabilities (pa,pb,1−pa−pb), and f(p)=max{0, min(pa−13, pb−13)}. Call the null the set where f=0: the union of the half-plane pa≤13 and the half-plane pb≤13. That is a non-convex set, and it is the right toy for the survey problem, whose null is a union over patterns of crossing direction (Chapter 16). The function is non-negative and piecewise linear. It is flat on the whole null, rises as a ramp across the quadrant pa>13, pb>13, and has a crease where the two ramps meet (Figure 15.1). The corner at (13,13) is on the boundary of the null, and at that point f′(h)=max{0,min(h1,h2)}, which is zero in three quarters of the directions and positive in the quarter where both coordinates rise.

15.2Sampling around the corner

Suppose the truth sits exactly at the corner, p0=(13,13), which is a point of the null with f(p0)=0. Draw n people from the three categories and form p^. By the multinomial central limit theorem n(p^−p0)→G, a Gaussian with variance 29 in each coordinate and covariance −19, so a correlation of −12. The function f is positively homogeneous about its corner, so nf^=f′(n(p^−p0)) with no remainder, and nf^ ⟶ f′(G)=max{0,min(G1,G2)}. This is not Gaussian. It is zero whenever G falls in the null side of the corner and positive on one quadrant, and so it has an atom at zero and a tail to the right. The probability that f^>0 is the probability that both coordinates of G are positive, P(G1>0,G2>0)=14+arcsin⁡ρ2π=16(ρ=−12),P(G1>0,G2>0)=14+arcsin⁡ρ2π=16(ρ=−12), which you can read as an angle: whiten G and the quadrant becomes a wedge of 60 degrees, and a spherical Gaussian puts 60 out of 360 of its mass there. The number does not contain n. Figure 15.2 shows a sample cloud and the law of nf^ at n=600.

Exact finite-n values from the same script show the limit arriving with a lattice wobble, since p^a>13 is a statement about integer counts:

n 30 100 300 1000 3000 10000
P(f^>0) 0.091 0.148 0.140 0.161 0.158 0.165

The limit is 16=0.167. Now move the truth a short way into the null, to (13−0.05, 13−0.05), and the same probability is 0.012 at n=30, 0.0028 at n=100, 1.4×10−5 at n=300 and about 3×10−12 at n=1000. Away from the boundary the rule declare incoherence when f^>0 works: it is a pointwise statement, true at every point of the null that is not on the boundary. On the boundary it settles at a probability set by an angle: one half along a straight edge, one sixth at the corner. And the zone where it has not yet become true shrinks only like n−1/2, so it is also what you meet in a finite sample whenever the truth is nearly on the edge, which is the case that matters.

Note what did not happen. f^ itself does shrink, like n−1/2. A positive f^ is a tiny number and not zero, and a statistic that is tiny is not the same as one that is zero. Cycle 17’s experiment 17c, below, finds exactly this in the real system.

For the survey tables the set of directions with C′>0 is a finite union of polyhedral cones in a space with many more dimensions than two, and the probability is its Gaussian mass. We did not compute that mass. The reviewer of cycle 17 did, directly: about 6 percent at the threshold with equal margins and about 19 percent at the hidden edges with drift 0.1 and 0.4, configurations of cycle 16 that the next sections describe. That the 6 percent is close to the nominal 5 percent is an accident of the geometry; nothing in the rule aims at it.

15.3What the bootstrap sees

The obvious repair is to calibrate: draw a bootstrap sample, compute the statistic, take a quantile. It does not work, and the reason is in the same picture.

Write the estimate as p^=p0+h/n, where h is where the cloud landed. A bootstrap sample is drawn around p^, not around p0: p∗=p^+G∗/n with G∗ the bootstrap analogue of G. In the toy, n{f(p∗)−f(p^)} ≈ f′(G∗+h)−f′(h), the bootstrap’s picture of the sampling law, and the target is f′(G). These two are the same law when h=0 and in general not otherwise. Figure 15.3 shows three positions of p^ and the 95th percentile of the bootstrap law at each. The numbers are from the Gaussian limit with two million draws, our computation:

Position h of the estimate (−0.9,−0.6) (0,0) (0.9,0.7)
95th percentile of f′(G∗+h)−f′(h) 0.00 0.19 0.29

The true 95th percentile of f′(G) is 0.19, the middle entry. At h=(0.15,0.10) the bootstrap gives 0.22, at (0.40,0.30) it gives 0.24. The bootstrap law moves with h, and h is random, so the bootstrap does not converge to anything fixed, let alone to the right thing.

What this does to a test is a separate question, and it came out less dramatic than we expected. We ran the standard bootstrap test on the toy, rejecting when nf^ exceeds the 95th percentile of n{f(p∗)−f(p^)}, with 300 resamples in each of 10,000 seeded datasets with the truth at the corner. It rejected 3.2 percent of the time at n=300 and 2.9 percent at n=1000. The same bootstrap applied to a linear statistic, p^a−13, rejected 4.5 and 4.8 percent; the Monte Carlo error is about 0.2 points. So in this toy the failure is conservative, and one line shows why. For an estimate inside the quadrant, f′(G∗+h)−f′(h)=max{0,min(G∗+h)}−min(h), and since min(u+v)≥min(u)+min(v) this is never stochastically smaller than min(G∗), so the bootstrap critical value is never below the true one. For an estimate in the null the statistic is zero, which cannot exceed a non-negative critical value, so there is no rejection to get wrong. That is a fact about this toy and not a theorem. The failure of the bootstrap is about the law; which way the test errs depends on the shape.

15.4What the papers say

What the paper says: Fang and Santos (2019), “Inference on directionally differentiable functions”

We read the abstract and Sections 3.2 and 3.3 of the arXiv version; the rest, including the applications and the local analysis, we did not. The setting is an estimator θ^n with a limit law and a map ϕ that is directionally but possibly not fully differentiable. The delta method still gives a limit for rn{ϕ(θ^n)−ϕ(θ0)}, namely ϕθ0′ applied to that limit. Theorem 3.1 says that when the limit is Gaussian with support a vector subspace, the standard bootstrap (the law of rn{ϕ(θ^n∗)−ϕ(θ^n)}) is consistent if and only if ϕ is fully differentiable at θ0. Corollary 3.1 gives the diagnostic: a non-Gaussian limiting distribution of the statistic means the standard bootstrap is inconsistent. Remark 3.2 records, from earlier work, an equivalent condition that needs no Gaussianity: the law of ϕ′(G+h)−ϕ′(h) must not depend on h, which is the check we made by hand in Figure 15.3. Section 3.3 offers a repair, composing an estimate of the directional derivative with the bootstrap, of which generalized moment selection is a special case; it also notes that m-out-of-n bootstrap and subsampling can remain valid. The paper does not treat the survey-table program, and the sections we read do not treat a linear program value. That C has a non-Gaussian limit on the boundary, and that this signals bootstrap failure there, is our application of the theorem. We have not checked that its formal assumptions hold for this problem, though the multinomial limit is Gaussian with a subspace as support, which is the part of the hypothesis one would look at first.

What the paper says: Kitamura and Stoye (2018), “Nonparametric analysis of random utility models”

We read the abstract, Sections 1 to 3.2 and 4.1 to 4.3 in full; we did not read Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 4.4 on, the Monte Carlo, the application or the appendices. Their test of a cone null uses a bootstrap that moves twice. The restricted estimate is tightened away from the boundary of the cone, with a tightening of order log⁡n/n in this project’s setting; bootstrap draws are recentered on that tightened estimate; and the bootstrap statistic is measured against the tightened cone. The paper calls the move of the center a double recentering, onto the null and again because the cone itself has been tightened. The paper is about random utility; applying its device to the shortfall is ours, and what exactly it requires is the subject of cycle 15 below.

What the paper says: Fang, Santos, Shaikh and Torgovitsky (2023), “Inference for large-scale linear systems with known coefficients”

We read the abstract, introduction and the statements in Section 3, and Section 4.1 afterwards; we did not read the proofs or the rest of Section 4. Their null is a vector equal to a known matrix times a non-negative vector. It matters here only because the cut-rule null is a finite union of such nulls, one per pattern of crossing directions; Chapter 16 builds the union test on that.

What the paper says: Hong and Li (2018), “The numerical delta method”

We could not obtain this paper (the publisher pages were blocked) and have only its metadata. It is recorded as the numerical-derivative alternative to Fang and Santos, and we cannot say what its step-size conditions are.

15.5What we found

Cycles 13 and 14: the first signs

Cycle 13 sampled the bracket [C^, C^+W^] of Chapter 14 with a bootstrap. It had no false alarms, and the estimate of the shortfall came out below its population value: 0.13 against 0.19 at n=1000 and 0.16 at n=4000, with no misreport. The identity explains it. Sampling noise makes the two copies of a margin differ, so W^ is 0.15 at n=1000 when the true gap is zero, and the cut rule lets that difference pay for incoherence just as it lets a drift. Noise acts as an admitted misreport. That is why the rule declare incoherence when C^>0 looked safe in the cells where margins are equal or nearly so.

Cycle 14 tried to narrow the bracket by correcting W^ for its sampling variance, and the corrected interval failed in a way that we now read as the first sighting of the kink. At n=1000 it raised false alarms in 96 percent of samples in the coherent cell, 98 percent with a drift of 0.4, and 94.5 percent in the hidden cell, where the reported tables have zero shortfall. The memo’s diagnosis was that where the cut rule finds no shortfall D=W holds as an equality, so D^ carries all the upward bias of W^, and subtracting a corrected W~ leaves a positive remainder that is only noise. The bias lives in the boundary between C=0 and C>0 and not in W alone. What survived was a hybrid that keeps cycle 13’s lower end and test and takes the debiased upper end; it adds no power.

Cycle 15: a calibration that did less than it appeared

Cycle 15 fitted a null-restricted version of the sample tables, and resampled from it. The null set was built by fixing a direction of crossing for each variable and cut; the directions were estimated from the sample, and the fit was a non-negative least squares problem in which every allowed joint outcome received at least τ/H of the mass, τ=log⁡n/n. Every fitted null had shortfall below 4×10−15. We used two statistics: T1=C^ and T2, the debiased lower end of cycle 14. The table gives percentages of 200 samples declared incoherent; the first four rows are false alarms, the last three power, and column A is the rule of cycle 13 on the same samples.

n=1000 n=4000
Case A T1 T2 A T1 T2
Coherent 0 0 19 0 0 16.5
Coherent, drift 0.4 0 0 9.5 0 0 9.5
Just coherent, w=0.32 0 0.5 21.5 0 0.5 15.5
Hidden, drift 0.4 0 4.5 18 0 0 16
Just incoherent, w=0.36 10 33 43.5 40 75 80.5
Incoherent, drift 0.2 93 100 100 100 100 100
Incoherent, drift 0.4 61 97 94 99 100 100

T2 was simply wrong: 9.5 to 21.5 percent false alarms. Our reading was that the fitted null keeps the sample’s margin gaps, mostly noise, as if they were real, so the correction removes less in the resamples than it did in the sample. T1 looked like a result: at most 4.5 percent false alarms, and power tripled near the threshold at n=1000. The table has one oddity that is only noise. Column A shows 61 percent in the last row where cycle 13 reported 54: same rule, different random draws, so comparisons are valid within a run and not across runs.

What the table hid was in the critical values. In a follow-up at n=1000 on six samples in each of three cells, with 100 null draws per sample, the 95th percentile of the null distribution was zero in all 18 samples inspected, and the share of null draws with C>0 was 0 to 3 percent in the hidden cell, where real sampling gave a positive C^ in 4.5 percent. The tightening pulled the fitted null inward, away from exactly the configurations where a positive C^ is likeliest. So the procedure’s validity in this cell was luck of design. The verdict we wrote then said that the rule’s false-alarm control came from the noise-induced downward bias and was checked only by simulation. It was a fair caveat and an inadequate one.

Cycle 16: the stress test

The rule is cheap to evaluate, so cycle 16 needed no bootstrap. It placed populations exactly on the boundary between C=0 and C>0, found by bisection, and counted how often C^>10−9. There were four designs, all with k=4 values: the structured system of cycle 10 at its threshold, w=13 with uniform margins; the same system with an upward drift and the pattern weight set to the largest value that the drift still hides (the hidden edge); random populations with their (Y,Z) table pushed toward reversal as far as C stays zero; and the threshold system with one survey much smaller than the others.

False alarms, percent n=200 1000 4000
Threshold, equal margins 5.3 4.8 5.5
Hidden edge, drift 0.05 8.3 10.5 13.5
Hidden edge, drift 0.1 7.5 13.8 18.8
Hidden edge, drift 0.2 14.8 15.0 16.8
Hidden edge, drift 0.4 24.3 16.5 19.3
Random boundary, diffuse: mean (max) 6.5 (14) 3.8 (13) 2.9 (9)
Random boundary, concentrated: mean (max) 10.7 (20) 8.7 (25) 6.4 (34)

The fixed designs use 400 samples each and the random rows use 40 populations with 100 samples each, so the maxima are inflated by selection. With one survey of 300 and two of 4,000 the threshold design gave 7.3 to 7.5 percent.

The rule fails. At the hidden edge it raises false alarms at 1.5 to 5 times the nominal level, 2 to 4 times from n=1000 on, and the rate does not fall as samples grow. (Our first write-up said “three to five times” and “up to 34 percent”. The review of cycle 17 corrected both. The 34 is the worst of the random populations, and the hidden-edge rates in the table run from 7.5 to 24.3.) A side note on the machine: two runs crashed because the solver reported infeasible programs for populations with entries near 10−300, which are feasible in exact arithmetic. We zeroed entries below 10−6 and renormalized and resumed from the saved results; no number already completed was changed.

Cycle 16 also diagnosed our adaptation. Kitamura and Stoye’s tightening goes with a recentered bootstrap, and we had used it with resampling from the tightened fit. Experiment 16b repeated the bootstrap without tightening, on 200 samples with 100 resamples:

Declares incoherent, percent Tightened Untightened
Hidden edge, drift 0.2, n=1000 (null) 19.0 2.5
Hidden edge, drift 0.4, n=200 (null) 18.5 1.5
Incoherent, drift 0.4, n=1000 (power) 97.5 55.0

Without tightening the critical value was positive in 71.5 to 99.5 percent of samples, the level came back in both null cells, and power fell to about where cycle 13’s rule had it. Cycle 15’s gain in power had been bought with false alarms. The notebook’s verdict withdrew “C^>0” and kept the bracket; the cycle-15 text was withdrawn, not deleted, so the record shows it.

Cycle 17: why, and how long it lasts

By the argument of the first sections, nC^ converges to C′(G)≥0 at a boundary point, with G the Gaussian limit of the scaled tables, and P(C^>0) converges to P(C′(G)>0), a constant fixed by the geometry of the point. That makes three predictions: the false-alarm rate stops falling, nC^ has an atom at zero with a stable share, and the upper quantiles of nC^ do not shrink. Cycle 17 tested each.

The rate settles. Experiment 17b ran the rule at n=16,000 and 64,000, 300 samples per cell, and Figure 15.4 joins those points to the cycle-16 rates (400 samples each at n=200, 1000, 4000):

At the hidden edge the rate settles between about 15 and 21 percent. With 300 samples the standard error at 19 percent is 2.3 points, and the six large-n estimates sit within 1.92 standard errors of the reviewer’s limits (our arithmetic; the farthest is drift 0.4 at n=16,000, which is 14.7 percent against 19). They do not distinguish the reviewer’s numbers from neighboring ones.

The law has an atom. Experiment 17c, at the hidden edge with drift 0.1 and 300 samples at each size:

n share with nC^=0 q90 q95 q99 max
1000 0.830 0.161 0.318 0.696 0.949
4000 0.817 0.239 0.428 0.696 1.281
16000 0.827 0.207 0.390 0.840 1.304
64000 0.817 0.277 0.566 0.965 1.134

The share at zero stays between 82 and 83 percent from n=1000 to 64,000, so P(C^>0) is 17 to 18.3 percent across those sizes, and the upper quantiles do not shrink. The 95th percentile runs between 0.3 and 0.6. With 300 samples the 95th and 99th percentiles are noisy, and a slow upward drift cannot be excluded by these data. The picture is an atom at zero plus a positive tail, which is what C′(G) should look like and what a Gaussian cannot be.

They are not solver artifacts. The rule declares incoherence when C^>10−9, and that is below the linear-program solver’s default feasibility tolerance of about 10−7. Experiment 17d scored the same 300 samples per cell at n=4000 at thresholds 10−9, 10−6 and 10−5. The rates were identical at all three: 3.3 percent at the threshold design, 19.0 percent at the hidden edge with drift 0.1 and 17.7 percent with drift 0.4. So in those samples C^ was either below 10−9 or above 10−5, nothing in between, which is what an atom and a tail predict. (The 3.3 percent at the threshold design is not the 5.5 percent of cycle 16 at the same n: different samples, with a standard error of about 1.2 points.)

Why cycle 15’s bootstrap missed it. Kitamura and Stoye make two moves: the draws are moved onto the tightened restricted estimate, and the bootstrap statistic is measured against the tightened cone. Cycle 15 also centered its resamples on the tightened fit, but measured the shortfall against the untightened null, so its resamples could not see the boundary. A quotation we had put into the notes for this sentence did not survive a check against the stored text of the paper. The sentence there names the cone by its symbol, and the second recentering it describes is the move of the center of the draws caused by the tightening, not the measurement against the tightened cone. The memo and the reading notes, corrected on November 14, now say the same.

An independent review of cycle 17 then checked these claims. It confirmed the identity D=W+2C, piecewise linearity and C′≥0 on the boundary, and the large-n evidence that P(C^>0) does not shrink. Three of its corrections concern this chapter: “three to five times” became 1.5 to 5; “up to 34 percent” was split into the hidden edge and the worst random population; and the statement that noise biases the shortfall down, which makes the test conservative, was restricted to equal or nearly equal margins, since at the hidden edge C^>0 in up to 26 percent of null samples across cycles 16 and 17. The directional-differentiability caveat described earlier we had already withdrawn in the notebook.

Where this leaves us

The rule “declare incoherence when C^>0” has power and no validity on the boundary of the null, and the boundary is where a drift has used up the slack in the margins. The reason is that C is non-negative and piecewise linear, so its derivative at the boundary is not linear, so nC^ has an atom at zero and a positive tail, which is a probability that C^>0 that does not shrink. None of this is new. The theorem linking directional differentiability to bootstrap failure is Fang and Santos’s, the boundary-of-the-null problem is the familiar problem of moment inequalities, and the identity belongs to Chapter 14. What the project adds is small: the observation that C=(D−W)/2 is non-negative and piecewise linear, so the boundary is exactly where the rule fails, and the simulations that show it. We have not established that nobody has made the observation before. Three repairs and what each costs are the subject of Chapter 16.
